title: al-Manṭiq
author: Shaykh Muḥammad Riḍā al-Muẓaffar (d. 1964)
description: First stage of the linked philosophy reading sequence. An original Arabic primary-source scan is available via Princeton/Arabic Collections Online. This reader contains an editorial study map and short source-checked translation excerpts; a complete new English translation is not yet present.

units.title: How this book prepares you for Bidāya and Nihāya
units.arabic: هذا دليل تحريري لقراءة كتاب المنطق، وليس ترجمة كاملة للنص. يُرجع إلى الأصل العربي في الروابط المذكورة، ويفصل بين نص المؤلف والتعليق.
units.english: Muẓaffar’s al-Manṭiq is the natural preparation for Ṭabāṭabāʾī’s two metaphysics books. First learn conception and assent; then the five predicables and definition; then predication, modal propositions, syllogism, and demonstration. In the shared reader, choose Book 1 to study logic, Book 2 for Bidāya, and Book 3 for Nihāya. The institutional Arabic scan contains the full original; the English units here are original editorial reading guides and selected short translations, not yet a complete translation.

notes.text: Original Arabic 1968 Najaf edition: Princeton / NYU ACO public-domain scan. A complete new English translation has not yet been written.

units.title: Conception, assent, and self-evident knowledge
units.english: Knowledge is divided into what is immediate or self-evident and what is reached through inquiry. This is an original translation of the heading, not the entire chapter. Distinguish conceiving a subject from assenting to a proposition: definition primarily addresses an unknown conception, while inference establishes an unknown judgment.

notes.text: Read Bidāya I.1: what it means for the concept of existence to be self-evident.

units.title: Meaning, signs, and expressions
units.english: Verbal signification. The corresponding chapter distinguishes how a linguistic expression signifies its meaning, its part, or a necessary concomitant. These matters are logically preparatory: they do not establish the existential reality of the thing signified.

units.title: Genus, differentia, species, and predication
units.arabic: النوع، الجنس، الفصل، الخاصة، العرض العام
units.english: Species, genus, differentia, proper attribute, and common accident: these five logical predicables are the building blocks for the theory of definition. In metaphysics, Ṭabāṭabāʾī denies that existence itself is a genus or differentia. This selection is a terminological guide, not a translation of Muẓaffar’s complete argument.

units.title: What can be defined? Four forms of definition
units.arabicTitle: الحد التام والناقص والرسم التام والناقص
units.arabic: الحد التام، الحد الناقص، الرسم التام، الرسم الناقص
units.english: Complete essential definition; incomplete essential definition; complete descriptive definition; incomplete descriptive definition. An essential definition draws on what belongs to the quiddity, whereas a description can distinguish a subject through its attributes. The concept of existence cannot be subjected to a genus–differentia definition. This is an original explanatory guide to the Arabic headings, not the complete translation.

notes.text: Read Bidāya I.1 and Nihāya I.2. Note that ḥadd in ḥudūd al-wujūd means delimitation, not automatically genus–differentia definition.

units.title: Predication and necessity, possibility, impossibility
units.arabic: الحمل الذاتي والشائع، الوجوب والإمكان والامتناع
units.english: Primary versus common predication must be kept distinct, especially when classifying a concept as what it means or considering its instance. Necessity, possibility, and impossibility also become modal determinations of propositions. This unit is a roadmap, not a complete translation.

units.title: Syllogistic inference
units.english: The categorical and hypothetical forms of inference show how a conclusion is warranted from prior propositions. This remains distinct from explaining what a term means and from the demonstration that a subject exists.

units.title: Demonstration and essential predication
units.english: Demonstration through the reason why and demonstration from a sign or effect are crucial to the later philosophical theory of science. Muẓaffar also distinguishes ‘essential’ in demonstrative science from the five-predicables sense. These are reading pointers, not the full authorial text.

notes.text: Advanced comparison: Ibn Sīnā, al-Shifāʾ, al-Burhān; see the logic dossier.

glossary.definition: An intelligible content considered without necessarily assenting to a judgment.
Cognition involving judgment that a proposition is true.
A specification of essential constituents; not to be confused with delimitation (ḥadd) in ontology.
Description using nonessential but distinctive attributes.
A rigorous inference yielding scientific certainty on the basis of appropriate premises.
